lead: A chemical sensor turns the concentration of one substance into an electrical signal. A biosensor is a chemical sensor with a biological layer in front of the transducer: the layer recognises one molecule and the transducer measures the change. The idea exists because a bare transducer reacts to many substances, while biology is selective. You meet these devices in a glucose strip, a home test kit ordered on UPI, a water-quality probe and a hospital blood-gas analyser.
prereq: You need sensitivity and selectivity from the static characteristics of sensors, and resistance or current change as a signal from resistive transducers. Device details follow in biosensor classes, ISFET, IMFET and glucose sensors.

blocks.text: The analyte is the substance being measured: glucose in blood, carbon monoxide in air, nitrate in water. Its amount is reported as a concentration, for example mmol/L or parts per million (ppm).

The recognition element is the part that binds or reacts with one analyte and largely ignores the rest. It can be a chemical layer such as a metal oxide or a solid electrolyte, or a biological molecule such as an enzyme. Some syllabi call it a bioreceptor or a receptor; those names mean the same thing.

The transducer converts the recognition event into a voltage, a current, a resistance or a light level that a circuit can read. The recognition element gives selectivity; the transducer gives the electrical output.

Classification uses two independent axes. By transducer: electrochemical, optical, acoustic, calorimetric. By biological element: enzyme, antibody, whole cell, DNA. A glucose strip, for example, is an enzyme biosensor with an amperometric transducer. Answer both axes when the question is open.

Electrochemical sensors are the largest family. In an amperometric sensor the electrode is held at a fixed voltage and the current is measured; current rises in proportion to concentration. In a potentiometric sensor ideally no current is drawn (a high-impedance meter reads the voltage) and the voltage follows the logarithm of concentration, as in a pH electrode. A conductometric sensor measures how the conductance of the solution changes as ions are produced.

blocks.where: I is the output current in nA; I₀ is the blank offset current in nA (the reading at zero analyte); S is the sensitivity in nA per mmol/L; C is the analyte concentration in mmol/L.

blocks.text: Optical sensors use absorbance (more analyte absorbs more light) or fluorescence (the analyte or a label emits light). Acoustic sensors use a quartz crystal microbalance or a surface acoustic wave device: mass landing on the surface shifts the resonant frequency. Details are in solid electrolyte and SAW sensors. Calorimetric sensors read the heat released by the reaction with a thermistor; the temperature rise depends on how much analyte reacted.

An enzyme sensor uses one enzyme that catalyses one reaction. Glucose oxidase oxidises glucose and produces hydrogen peroxide; the peroxide is oxidised at an electrode and gives a current proportional to glucose. The enzyme supplies the selectivity, so other sugars in blood barely respond.

An immunosensor uses an antibody that binds one antigen, the molecule it was raised against. Binding changes mass, light or charge at the surface, and that change is transduced. Pregnancy strips and pathogen tests work this way. The binding is strong and specific but slow compared with an enzyme reaction.

A microbial or whole-cell sensor uses living cells as the recognition element. The cells are cheap and tolerate harsh samples but respond slowly. A DNA sensor uses a short probe strand that hybridises with the target strand; the hybrid is read optically or electrochemically.

Advantages: high selectivity, fast response for enzyme devices, and a low sample volume — one drop of blood is enough. Limitations: short shelf life because enzymes denature, drift with time, sensitivity to temperature, fouling of the electrode surface, and the need for regular calibration. A smart sensor package can hold the calibration curve and correct drift, as in smart sensors.

In medicine each class has a bedside use. Enzyme electrodes measure glucose and lactate in blood; potentiometric ion-selective electrodes measure Na⁺, K⁺ and pH in a blood-gas analyser; antibody (immuno) sensors in lateral-flow strips detect pregnancy hormone, cardiac troponin after a heart attack and viral antigens; and DNA sensors detect a pathogen's genes. The choice of element sets what is detected; the choice of transducer sets how the signal is read.

spec.aria: Five blocks from sample through glucose oxidase, platinum electrode and conditioning to the display, and a straight calibration line of current against glucose through two standards, with a sample at 120 nanoamperes reading 7.0 millimoles per litre.

examples.question: An amperometric glucose biosensor has a blank offset current of 5 nA and a sensitivity of 20 nA per mmol/L. A blood sample reads 4.5 mmol/L glucose. Find the output current.
steps: Write the linear model: I = I₀ + S·C.
Identify the blank offset: I₀ = 5 nA. This is the reading with zero glucose, not an error.
Multiply: S·C = 20 × 4.5 = 90 nA. The units cancel as (nA/(mmol/L)) × mmol/L = nA.
Add the offset: I = 5 nA + 90 nA = 95 nA.

examples.question: A glucose biosensor is calibrated with two standards. A 2.0 mmol/L standard gives 45 nA and a 10.0 mmol/L standard gives 165 nA. (a) Find the sensitivity S and the blank current I₀. (b) A fasting patient's sample then gives 120 nA. Find the glucose concentration in mmol/L and in mg/dL (1 mmol/L of glucose = 18.0 mg/dL), and say whether it lies in the normal fasting range of 3.9 to 5.5 mmol/L.
steps: The sensor is linear: I = I₀ + S·C. Two standards give two equations, enough for the two unknowns S and I₀.
Blank: I₀ = 45 − 15 × 2.0 = 45 − 30 = 15 nA. Check with the other standard: 15 + 15 × 10.0 = 165 nA, as measured.
Invert the model for the sample: C = (I − I₀)/S = (120 − 15)/15 = 105/15 = 7.0 mmol/L.

Compare: 7.0 mmol/L is above the normal fasting range of 3.9 to 5.5 mmol/L; a fasting value of 7.0 mmol/L or more on repeat tests is the usual threshold for diabetes. The meter only reports; the diagnosis is the doctor's.
examples.answer: S = 15 nA per mmol/L and I₀ = 15 nA. The sample is 7.0 mmol/L, or 126 mg/dL, which is above the normal fasting range.

traps: Calling every chemical sensor a biosensor. A biosensor must have a biological recognition element; a metal-oxide gas sensor does not.
Answering with the transducer when the question asks for the biological element, or the reverse. Give both axes when the wording is open.
Swapping amperometric and potentiometric. Amperometric: fixed voltage, measure current. Potentiometric: zero current, measure voltage.
Dropping the blank offset I₀. For 4.5 mmol/L at 20 nA/(mmol/L) the current is 95 nA, not 90 nA.
Saying an acoustic sensor measures mass directly. It measures a frequency shift, which is converted to mass using the calibration.
Calibrating with one standard only. One point fixes neither the slope nor the blank; a meter needs two standards, or a known zero and one standard, before a sample reading means anything.

quiz.a: The analyte is the substance being measured, for example glucose in blood. The recognition element is the layer that binds or reacts with that analyte and gives the sensor its selectivity.

quiz.q: Name the two axes used to classify biosensors.
quiz.a: By transducer (electrochemical, optical, acoustic, calorimetric) and by biological element (enzyme, antibody, whole cell, DNA).

quiz.q: Why does adding an enzyme layer improve the selectivity of a glucose sensor?
quiz.a: Glucose oxidase reacts with glucose and not with other sugars in blood, and turns it into hydrogen peroxide. The electrode oxidises that peroxide, so its current comes only from glucose that the enzyme has converted. The selectivity comes from the enzyme, not from the electrode.

quiz.q: State one difference between amperometric and potentiometric sensing.
quiz.a: Amperometric holds the electrode at a fixed voltage and measures current, which is linear in concentration. Potentiometric draws ideally no current and measures voltage, which follows the logarithm of concentration.

quiz.q: An amperometric sensor has I₀ = 2 nA and S = 15 nA/(mmol/L). The sample reads 6 mmol/L. Find the output current.
A glucose strip has a shelf life of six months even though the electrode is stable for years. Explain.
quiz.a: The enzyme is the weak part. Proteins denature with heat and time, so the recognition layer loses activity. The electrode is stable but the enzyme limits the strip.

quiz.q: A water-quality biosensor drifts upward after 30 days in the stream. Name two likely causes and one fix.
quiz.a: Fouling of the membrane or electrode by biofilm, and temperature change altering enzyme activity or membrane permeability. Fix: clean or replace the membrane and recalibrate against a standard, or fit temperature compensation in the smart-sensor electronics.

beyond: Not for the exam. Wearable sweat sensors and continuous glucose monitors put the same two-axis design into a patch on the arm. Labs are replacing enzymes with aptamers, short DNA strands that bind like antibodies, to get longer shelf life. Paper microfluidics makes single-use strips cheap enough for village clinics. Search 'aptamer biosensor', 'lateral flow assay' and 'continuous glucose monitor enzyme electrode'.
